REASONS FOR DECISION

[1] XXXX XXXX (the claimant) is a citizen of the People's Republic of China. He claims to have a well-founded fear of persecution at the hands of the Communist regime and in particular, the Public Security Bureau, by reason of his practice of Falun Gong under sections 96 and 97 of The Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.1
ALLEGATIONS

[2] The claimant alleges in his Personal Information Form (PIF)2 that as a result of a XXXX XXXX, he turned to Falun Gong on the recommendation of an aunt. The claimant maintains that he started to practice Falun Gong in XXXX 2011. On XXXX XXXX, 2012, the claimant's Falun Gong practice group was raided by the Public Security Bureau (the PSB). The claimant stated that upon the advice of his mother, he went into hiding at the home of a relative. The claimant alleges that the Public Security Bureau (the PSB) have gone to his home to search for him. A snakehead (smuggler) was hired to take him out of the People's Republic of China. The claimant came to Canada on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2012, and filed for refugee protection a few days later.
DETERMINATION

[3] I find that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. I am cognizant of the difficulties faced by the claimant in establishing his claim, including cultural factors, the milieu of the hearing room and the stress inherent in responding to oral questions. I have taken these considerations into account in arriving at negative credibility findings.
Identity

subthemes.text:
[4] The claimant's oral testimony and the supporting documents filed3 establish his identity as a national of the People's Republic of China.
The claimant as a Falun Gong practitioner in the People's Republic of China

[5] I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant was not a Falun Gong practitioner in the People's Republic of China.

[6] The claimant was able to use his genuine Chinese passport to leave the People's Republic of China. Moreover, the claimant was successfully able to hide in the People's Republic of China for two and a half months. The claimant also indicated that the PSB did not leave any summons with his family, although having attended on more than one occasion. If the claimant was truly wanted by the PSB, a summons would have been left at his home with his parents. I give the letter4 from the school dismissal no weight since it contains no security features and I have already found the claimant was not a Falun Gong practitioner in the People's Republic of China. I give no weight to the letter5 from the claimant's mother as I find it is self-serving.
Ability to leave the People's Republic of China with his genuine passport

[7] I have also considered the Chairperson's Jurisprudential Guide TB6-11632.6 I have also considered the opposing case law such as the recent decision in Huang v. MCI7 wherein Russell J. outlined case law and opposing arguments that must be considered when assessing a claimant's ability to leave the People's Republic of China on his or her own genuine passport. Among those arguments stated in the case law are the following key points: (a) That a well-placed bribe to an official with a computer may be sufficient to compromise the Golden Shield system, thereby permitting a claimant to leave the People's Republic of China undetected; and (b) Whereas corruption is endemic in the People's Republic of China, it is plausible for a snakehead (smuggler) may successfully help a claimant bypass the Golden Shield police computer system and authorities. I have reviewed TB6-11632 and find that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) did address and consider this opposing case law and these specific arguments.8 The RAD in TB6-11632 outlined extensive evidence in the national documentation package about exit controls in the People's Republic of China. Many of these exit controls were in place when the claimant left the country. I find that the claimant's description of his flight from the People's Republic of China is not consistent with that as described in the national documentation evidence. The claimant was quite vague with respect as to his ability to leave the People's Republic of China: he indicated that he did not know how he was able to leave the country although the Golden Shield computer system was in place.

[8] I have also considered the opposing arguments regarding bribery and endemic corruption in the People's Republic of China. These arguments do not address my concerns in the current case as outlined in the previous paragraph. Where the claimant himself is not credible with respect to his travel through the airport, arguments about bribery and corruption make little difference. I adopt the reasoning of the RAD in TB6-11632. While it is plausible or possible that a wanted fugitive may be smuggled out of the People's Republic of China, I need not accept it or believe it to be probable in the current case. In the current case, given the claimant's lack of credibility about being a Falun Gong practitioner, I find it unlikely that he was smuggled out of the country. I therefore find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant did not leave the People's Republic of China as he described using his own genuine Chinese passport. I therefore find that the claimant is not being sought by the Chinese authorities for being a Falun Gong practitioner.

[9] In conclusion, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant was never a Falun Gong practitioner in the People's Republic of China and has never been wanted by Chinese authorities.
The claimant as a Falun Gong practitioner in Canada

[10] The claimant testified that he started to practice Falun Gong in the People's Republic of China in XXXX 2011, and would practice three to four times a week. The claimant came to Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2012, and indicated that he practiced Falun Gong for three months only.

[11] The claimant was asked if he had read Zhuan Falun and he replied in the affirmative. The claimant was asked if Master Li describes how to perform the exercises in Zhuan Falun, to which he replied in the affirmative. That answer is incorrect and I find, on a balance of probabilities that the claimant has never read Zhuan Falun as a description of how to perform the exercises would take several pages. The claimant was able to say that there were five exercises and was partially correct when asked as to what evil cultivation was, indicating that it was black substance, although unable to indicate that it is people seeking fame or fortune. The claimant was asked to name the exercises, but was unable to do so. The claimant was asked to demonstrate the first exercise, but was unable to do so. The claimant was asked to recite one of the verses, but was unable to do so. When it was pointed out to the claimant that the principles of Falun Gong are truth, compassion and forbearance. The claimant was asked what truth meant. The claimant stated that truth is about your own nature. This answer is incorrect. Truth means telling the truth about Falun Gong - its benefits and how the Chinese government has persecuted Falun Gong practitioners.

[12] I am cognizant of Federal Court jurisprudence which cautions against determining religious identity on the basis of a refugee's religious knowledge or lack thereof. However, it is important to recognize that, unlike religions in general, which are faith-based, the objective evidence establishes that knowledge is an important component of Falun Gong.
The foundation of Falun Dafa [Falun Gong] consists of a body of fundamental knowledge essential for the task of undertaking proper cultivation towards higher stages of attainment. It comprises Master Li's teaching collected in a number of books, the most important being Zhuan Falun (Revolving the Law Wheel).9 (emphasis added)

subthemes.text:
[13] It is clear that the claimant knows next to nothing about Falun Gong. His explanation is that he has not practised Falun Gong for a number of years. However, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant should remember something about it since he practised it three to four times a week for over a year. The claimant came to Canada on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2012, and only practised Falun Gong for the first three months, three or four times a week after his arrival. When the claimant came to Canada, he did not want to practice Falun Gong in public because there are Chinese spies. The claimant stated that he was afraid of Chinese spies in Canada which might affect his parents. I reject this explanation. The claimant had testified that the PSB already knew of his alleged practice of Falun Gong in the People's Republic of China as of XXXX XXXX, 2012, and therefore, it would not make any difference if Chinese officials knew of his Falun Gong practice in Canada since he was allegedly wanted in the People's Republic of China. When asked as to why he did not practice Falun Gong in the privacy of his home, the claimant indicated that his mother told him not to practice until he obtained status here in Canada and then he could resume practising. I reject this explanation: I find it neither credible nor plausible: the reason he came to Canada was to allegedly afraid of being arrested by the PSB and the ability to practice Falun Gong freely. Furthermore, it would not make any difference if the claimant had status in Canada or not: he could practice Falun Gong freely and without fear in Canada. I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant is not, nor has ever been a Falun Gong practitioner in the People's Republic of China or in Canada.
CONCLUSION

Among those arguments stated in the case law are the following key points: (a) That a well-placed bribe to an official with a computer may be sufficient to compromise the Golden Shield system, thereby permitting a claimant to leave the People's Republic of China undetected; and (b) Whereas corruption is endemic in the People's Republic of China, it is plausible for a snakehead (smuggler) may successfully help a claimant bypass the Golden Shield police computer system and authorities. I have reviewed TB6-11632 and find that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) did address and consider this opposing case law and these specific arguments.8 The RAD in TB6-11632 outlined extensive evidence in the national documentation package about exit controls in the People's Republic of China. Many of these exit controls were in place when the claimant left the country. I find that the claimant's description of his flight from the People's Republic of China is not consistent with that as described in the national documentation evidence. The claimant was quite vague with respect as to his ability to leave the People's Republic of China: he indicated that he did not know how he was able to leave the country although the Golden Shield computer system was in place.

[8] I have also considered the opposing arguments regarding bribery and endemic corruption in the People's Republic of China. These arguments do not address my concerns in the current case as outlined in the previous paragraph. Where the claimant himself is not credible with respect to his travel through the airport, arguments about bribery and corruption make little difference. I adopt the reasoning of the RAD in TB6-11632. While it is plausible or possible that a wanted fugitive may be smuggled out of the People's Republic of China, I need not accept it or believe it to be probable in the current case. In the current case, given the claimant's lack of credibility about being a Falun Gong practitioner, I find it unlikely that he was smuggled out of the country. I therefore find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant did not leave the People's Republic of China as he described using his own genuine Chinese passport. I therefore find that the claimant is not being sought by the Chinese authorities for being a Falun Gong practitioner.

[9] In conclusion, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant was never a Falun Gong practitioner in the People's Republic of China and has never been wanted by Chinese authorities.
The claimant as a Falun Gong practitioner in Canada

[10] The claimant testified that he started to practice Falun Gong in the People's Republic of China in XXXX 2011, and would practice three to four times a week. The claimant came to Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2012, and indicated that he practiced Falun Gong for three months only.

[11] The claimant was asked if he had read Zhuan Falun and he replied in the affirmative. The claimant was asked if Master Li describes how to perform the exercises in Zhuan Falun, to which he replied in the affirmative. That answer is incorrect and I find, on a balance of probabilities that the claimant has never read Zhuan Falun as a description of how to perform the exercises would take several pages. The claimant was able to say that there were five exercises and was partially correct when asked as to what evil cultivation was, indicating that it was black substance, although unable to indicate that it is people seeking fame or fortune. The claimant was asked to name the exercises, but was unable to do so. The claimant was asked to demonstrate the first exercise, but was unable to do so. The claimant was asked to recite one of the verses, but was unable to do so. When it was pointed out to the claimant that the principles of Falun Gong are truth, compassion and forbearance. The claimant was asked what truth meant. The claimant stated that truth is about your own nature. This answer is incorrect. Truth means telling the truth about Falun Gong - its benefits and how the Chinese government has persecuted Falun Gong practitioners.

[12] I am cognizant of Federal Court jurisprudence which cautions against determining religious identity on the basis of a refugee's religious knowledge or lack thereof. However, it is important to recognize that, unlike religions in general, which are faith-based, the objective evidence establishes that knowledge is an important component of Falun Gong.
The foundation of Falun Dafa [Falun Gong] consists of a body of fundamental knowledge essential for the task of undertaking proper cultivation towards higher stages of attainment. It comprises Master Li's teaching collected in a number of books, the most important being Zhuan Falun (Revolving the Law Wheel).9 (emphasis added)

[13] It is clear that the claimant knows next to nothing about Falun Gong. His explanation is that he has not practised Falun Gong for a number of years. However, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant should remember something about it since he practised it three to four times a week for over a year. The claimant came to Canada on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2012, and only practised Falun Gong for the first three months, three or four times a week after his arrival. When the claimant came to Canada, he did not want to practice Falun Gong in public because there are Chinese spies. The claimant stated that he was afraid of Chinese spies in Canada which might affect his parents. I reject this explanation. The claimant had testified that the PSB already knew of his alleged practice of Falun Gong in the People's Republic of China as of XXXX XXXX, 2012, and therefore, it would not make any difference if Chinese officials knew of his Falun Gong practice in Canada since he was allegedly wanted in the People's Republic of China. When asked as to why he did not practice Falun Gong in the privacy of his home, the claimant indicated that his mother told him not to practice until he obtained status here in Canada and then he could resume practising. I reject this explanation: I find it neither credible nor plausible: the reason he came to Canada was to allegedly afraid of being arrested by the PSB and the ability to practice Falun Gong freely. Furthermore, it would not make any difference if the claimant had status in Canada or not: he could practice Falun Gong freely and without fear in Canada. I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant is not, nor has ever been a Falun Gong practitioner in the People's Republic of China or in Canada.
CONCLUSION

[14] I therefore determine that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. The Refugee Protection Division therefore rejects his claim.
